chapter.title: Build it from what they already know

cards.body: Why does saying your point three times make a talk clearer, not more boring? Because a listener can't flip back a page. When you lead a hike, you don't start the trail at your own front door. You **start where your group is standing**, and you point at the summit again at every bend.
cards.simpler: Why does saying your point three times make a talk clearer, not more boring? Because people listening can't turn back a page. Think of leading a group on a hike. You don't begin the walk at your own front door. You **start where your group is standing**. Then, at every bend in the path, you point at the top again.

cards.prompt: You're giving a 5-minute talk about a new budgeting app to 30 nurses. Where should your first example come from?

options.text: The app's settings screen, so they see the real thing
The shift rota they argue about every week
How your own team uses the app at the office

whyNot.a: That's your trailhead, not theirs: they've never seen that screen, so they have nothing to build on yet.
whyNot.c: That's your life, not theirs: your office is as unfamiliar to them as their ward is to you.

cards.reteach: People rebuild your idea out of pieces they already own. A nurse owns the rota, the handover and the 3 a.m. break. They don't own your app yet. Start where they're standing, then walk them over to it.

cards.title: Their bricks, not yours
cards.body:
Chris Anderson's view is that you can't hand an idea over whole. The listener rebuilds it in their own head, using only pieces they already have: their job, their kitchen, their commute.

So **every example should come from the listener's life**, not yours. You'd think clever people want clever examples. It's the reverse. A surgeon still gets a supermarket queue faster than your industry's jargon.

And give them a reason to care before the detail. Nobody studies the trail map until they know the view at the top is worth the climb.
cards.simpler: Chris Anderson says you can't hand over an idea whole. The listener rebuilds it in their own head from parts they already have, like their job, their kitchen or their commute. So **every example should come from the listener's life**, not yours. That goes for clever people too. A surgeon gets a supermarket queue faster than your work's special words. Show why it matters first. Nobody reads the trail map until they know the view at the top is worth the climb.

cards.title: The gym that earns you
cards.body: Mei is an accountant. Her cousin Leo, a bike courier, asks what *accrual* means. Her first answer, "recording income when it's earned, not when it's paid", gets a blank look. Her second answer starts **from his life**: you pay your gym £360 in January for the whole year, but the gym only earns £30 of it each month you could walk in. Leo, who has been twice since March: "So they've been earning me all year and I've been earning nothing."
cards.simpler: Mei is an accountant. Her cousin Leo, a bike courier, asks what *accrual* means. Her first answer, "recording income when it's earned, not when it's paid", gets a blank stare. Her second answer starts **from his life**. You pay your gym £360 in January for the year, but the gym only earns £30 of it each month you could walk in. Leo has been twice since March: "So they've been earning me all year and I've been earning nothing."

cards.what: TED's secret to great public speaking
cards.watchFor: Listen for where he says to build the idea step by step out of things the audience already understands. That's today's chapter.

cards.prompt: Dev writes software. His mum, a primary school teacher, asks what *version control* is. Which explanation starts where she's standing?

options.text: "It's basically like Git, just the general idea."
"It's like saving every draft of a school report with the date on it, so you can go back to Tuesday's if Thursday's goes wrong."
"It tracks changes across commits in a shared repository."

whyNot.a: That's Dev's world, not hers: she's never seen Git, so "like Git" points at nothing.
whyNot.c: That's a definition, not a way in: three new words, and none of them explained.

cards.reteach: A good example is made of the listener's own things. A teacher already knows drafts, dates, and the panic of losing Thursday's version. Build from those, and the new word has somewhere to land.

cards.title: They can't flip back
cards.body:
A listener has no rewind button. With a book you can flip back a page. In a talk, each sentence is gone the moment it ends.

That changes two things. First, explain every new word **in the same breath** you first say it: "churn, meaning customers who leave". Leave it two minutes and people have stopped trying.

Second, say your one idea more than once. Patrick Winston calls this *cycling*: come back to it about three times, because at any moment someone in the room is thinking about lunch. It isn't padding. It's the next trail marker.
cards.simpler: People listening can't rewind. In a book you can turn back a page, but in a talk each sentence is gone once it ends. So explain each new word **in the same breath** you first say it: "churn, meaning customers who leave". Wait two minutes and people have given up. Also, come back to your one idea about three times. Patrick Winston calls this *cycling*. At any moment, someone is thinking about lunch. It isn't padding. It's the next trail marker.

cards.body: Tom, a network engineer, explains to parents at his kid's school why the Wi-Fi is slow. He says *latency* eight times before he explains it, four minutes in. By then the parents have filed it under "tech stuff" and picked up their phones. How to catch it: read your talk to a friend outside your field and ask them to tap the table at **every word they'd have to look up**.
cards.simpler: Tom works on computer networks. He tells parents at his kid's school why the Wi-Fi is slow. He says *latency* eight times before he explains it, four minutes in. By then the parents have decided it's "tech stuff" and picked up their phones. To catch this, read your talk to a friend who works in something else. Ask them to tap the table at **every word they'd have to look up**.

cards.prompt: After your talk, Priya says: "I followed every sentence, but I couldn't tell you what it was about." What most likely went wrong?

options.text: You said your one idea three times
Your examples and words came from your world, so she had nothing of her own to hang them on
You gave a reason to care before the detail

whyNot.a: That's cycling, and it helps: anyone who drifted gets a second and third chance to catch the point.
whyNot.c: That's the order that works: people climb harder once they know the view is worth it.

cards.reteach: Following the sentences isn't the same as building the idea. If every piece came from your job, the listener nods along and takes nothing home. Use pieces from their life and the idea stays standing after you stop talking.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
People can only build your idea out of what they already have, so **take your examples from their life** and explain each new word the moment you say it. They can't rewind, so say the one idea about three times. That's a trail marker, not padding.

Tomorrow: your voice, and why a 3-second pause is a tool, not a mistake.
cards.simpler: People can only build your idea from what they already have. So **take your examples from their life**, and explain each new word the moment you say it. They can't rewind, so say your one idea about three times. That isn't padding. It's a trail marker, like the signs that keep walkers on the path. Tomorrow: your voice, and why a three-second pause is a tool, not a mistake.

cards.body: Tonight, explain one word from your work to someone outside it, in person or by text. Build it from one thing in their day, not yours. Notice whether they ask a follow-up question or just nod.
cards.simpler: Tonight, explain one word from your work to someone who doesn't do your job. You can do it face to face or by text. Build it from **one thing in their day**, not yours. Then watch what happens. Do they ask a follow-up question, or do they just nod?

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now explain one idea from your work to someone outside it, using 2 examples from their life, not yours.
